text: Iron toxicity, often called "bronzing" (ចំនួពុលជាតិដែក, "chomngu pul cheat dèk"), isn't caused by a pathogen - it's a soil/nutrient problem the source lists alongside true diseases because the visible symptoms look similar to farmers. Leaves develop small brown-to-orange spots that, as the problem worsens, spread and turn the whole leaf a bronze/rust color; affected hills are stunted with poor tillering. The source links this to naturally iron-rich acid soils and to poorly drained fields, where iron stays in a form roots take up in excess. Management is about the soil and water rather than spraying anything: improve field drainage so soil isn't waterlogged for extended stretches, and on fields known to run iron-heavy, keep phosphorus and potassium nutrition adequate - shortfalls in either of those make iron-toxicity symptoms worse, so correcting them helps the crop tolerate background iron levels better even without changing the iron itself.
